solutions.21: A vector perpendicular to both is parallel to a⃗ × b⃗. Now a⃗ × b⃗ = |î ĵ k̂; 1 2 3; 2 −1 1| = 5î + 5ĵ − 5k̂ = 5(î + ĵ − k̂). Its magnitude is 5√3. Therefore the two required unit vectors are ±(î + ĵ − k̂)/√3.

solutions.18: Let a⃗ = î + 2ĵ + 2k̂ and b⃗ = 2î + ĵ − 2k̂. Their dot product is 2 + 2 − 4 = 0. Since both are non-zero, cos θ = 0 and the angle is θ = π/2.
solutions.19: A point on the first line is (1 + λ, λ, 1), while a point on the second is (μ, 1 − μ, 1). Equality of coordinates requires 1 + λ = μ and λ = 1 − μ. Substitution gives λ = 0 and μ = 1. Both lines therefore contain (1, 0, 1), so they intersect there.
solutions.20: AB⃗ = (4 − 1)î + (6 − 2)ĵ + (3 − 3)k̂ = 3î + 4ĵ, and |AB⃗| = 5. Thus the direction cosines are 3/5, 4/5 and 0. A vector equation is r⃗ = (î + 2ĵ + 3k̂) + λ(3î + 4ĵ). The Cartesian equations are (x − 1)/3 = (y − 2)/4 with z = 3.
solutions.21: Take a⃗₁ = î, a⃗₂ = ĵ and b⃗ = î + 2ĵ + 2k̂. Then a⃗₂ − a⃗₁ = −î + ĵ and (a⃗₂ − a⃗₁) × b⃗ = 2î + 2ĵ − 3k̂. Therefore the distance is √(4 + 4 + 9)/√(1 + 4 + 4) = √17/3.
solutions.22: The direction vectors b⃗₁ = î + ĵ and b⃗₂ = î + k̂ are not proportional. Also b⃗₁ × b⃗₂ = î − ĵ − k̂. With a⃗₂ − a⃗₁ = −î + ĵ + k̂, the scalar product (a⃗₂ − a⃗₁) · (b⃗₁ × b⃗₂) = −3 ≠ 0. The lines are therefore non-coplanar and hence skew. Their shortest distance is |−3|/√3 = √3.
solutions.23: The direction vectors are b⃗₁ = (1, 1, 0) and b⃗₂ = (0, 1, 1), so b⃗₁ × b⃗₂ = (1, −1, 1). With a⃗₂ − a⃗₁ = (−1, 1, 1), the scalar triple product is −1 ≠ 0; hence the lines are skew. Let P = (1 + λ, λ, 0) on L₁ and Q = (0, 1 + μ, 1 + μ) on L₂. For PQ⃗ to be perpendicular to both directions, μ − 2λ = 0 and 2 + 2μ − λ = 0. Thus λ = −⅔ and μ = −⁴⁄₃. Therefore P = (⅓, −⅔, 0), Q = (0, −⅓, −⅓), and PQ = √[(−⅓)² + (⅓)² + (−⅓)²] = 1/√3 = √3/3.
solutions.24: (a) The direction vector is 2î − ĵ + 2k̂, whose magnitude is 3. Its direction cosines are ⅔, −⅓, ⅔. (b) The paths have the same direction vector and different initial points, so they are distinct parallel lines. (c) Let d⃗ = (3, 1, 2) − (1, 2, 1) = 2î − ĵ + k̂ and b⃗ = 2î − ĵ + 2k̂. Then d⃗ × b⃗ = −î − 2ĵ. Hence the shortest distance is |d⃗ × b⃗|/|b⃗| = √5/3 metres.

solutions.20: Let D be the event that a component is defective. By total probability, P(D) = P(X)P(D | X) + P(Y)P(D | Y) = 0.60(0.02) + 0.40(0.05) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032 = ⁴⁄₁₂₅.
solutions.22: There are C(52, 2) = 1326 unordered pairs of cards. A favourable pair is formed by choosing 1 of 4 aces and 1 of 4 kings, giving 4×4 = 16 pairs. Hence the probability is 16/1326 = ⁸⁄₆₆₃.
solutions.23: Let R denote a red ball. By total probability, P(R) = (½)(⅖) + (⅓)(⅘) + (⅙)(⅗) = ⅕ + ⁴⁄₁₅ + ¹⁄₁₀ = ¹⁷⁄₃₀. For Box II, P(II | R) = [(⅓)(⅘)]/(¹⁷⁄₃₀) = (⁴⁄₁₅)(³⁰⁄₁₇) = ⁸⁄₁₇. The joint probability of choosing Box I or III and obtaining red is ⅕ + ¹⁄₁₀ = ³⁄₁₀, so P(I or III | R) = (³⁄₁₀)/(¹⁷⁄₃₀) = ⁹⁄₁₇.
solutions.24: (a) P(D ∩ +) = P(D)P(+ | D) = 0.02×0.95 = 0.019. (b) P(+) = 0.02(0.95) + 0.98(0.04) = 0.019 + 0.0392 = 0.0582. (c) By Bayes’ theorem, P(D | +) = 0.019/0.0582 = ⁹⁵⁄₂₉₁ ≈ 0.3265. Thus only about 32.65% of positive results represent people who actually have the condition; the lower value is caused by false positives in the much larger unaffected group.

notes.subtitle: Components, Products, Projections & Areas

concepts.title: Vectors and components
concepts.text: A vector has magnitude and direction. In three dimensions, a⃗ = a₁î + a₂ĵ + a₃k̂ and |a⃗| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²). Equal vectors have equal corresponding components.

concepts.title: Position and section vectors
concepts.text: The position vector locates a point from the origin. If P divides AB internally in the ratio m : n, then OP⃗ is the weighted average [mOB⃗ + nOA⃗]/(m + n).

concepts.title: Scalar product
concepts.text: The dot product measures directional alignment. It finds angles, tests perpendicularity, and gives scalar or vector projections.

concepts.title: Vector product
concepts.text: The cross product is perpendicular to both factors. Its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram determined by the vectors; half of it is the corresponding triangle area.

formulas: |a⃗| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²); a unit vector along a⃗ is a⃗/|a⃗|
If AP : PB = m : n, OP⃗ = [mOB⃗ + nOA⃗]/(m + n)
a⃗ · b⃗ = |a⃗||b⃗| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃
Scalar projection of a⃗ on b⃗ = (a⃗ · b⃗)/|b⃗|
Vector projection of a⃗ on b⃗ = [(a⃗ · b⃗)/|b⃗|²]b⃗
|a⃗ × b⃗| = |a⃗||b⃗| sin θ
Parallelogram area = |a⃗ × b⃗|; triangle area = ½|a⃗ × b⃗|
î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ; reversing the order changes the sign
method: Write every vector in component form and preserve the order of coordinates.
Choose the dot product for angles, perpendicularity and projection; choose the cross product for a common perpendicular or area.
For a division point, identify which weight multiplies each endpoint before substituting.
Check a result through magnitude, direction and units; a unit vector must have magnitude 1.

example.question: Find the area of the triangle whose adjacent side vectors are a⃗ = î + ĵ and b⃗ = î + k̂.
steps: Compute a⃗ × b⃗ = (î + ĵ) × (î + k̂) = î − ĵ − k̂.
A triangle has half the area of the parallelogram on the same two vectors.

practice.question: Find the magnitude of 3î − 4ĵ + 12k̂.
Find a unit vector along 2î − 2ĵ + k̂.
Find the angle between î + ĵ and î − ĵ.
Find the projection of 2î + 3ĵ on î + ĵ.
practice.answer: Scalar projection = 5/√2; vector projection = ⁵⁄₂(î + ĵ).

practice.question: Find the area of the parallelogram on î + 2ĵ and 2î + k̂.
A(1, 2, −1), B(7, −1, 5); find the point dividing AB internally in the ratio 2 : 1.

tips: The dot product is a scalar; the cross product is a vector.
For b⃗ × a⃗, reverse the sign of a⃗ × b⃗.
Use |b⃗|², not |b⃗|, in the vector-projection formula.
Scalar triple product and equations of planes are outside the current chapter scope.

notes.subtitle: Lines, Angles, Intersections & Shortest Distance

concepts.title: Direction ratios and cosines
concepts.text: Any non-zero proportional triple gives direction ratios of a line. Dividing a direction vector by its magnitude gives direction cosines l, m and n satisfying l² + m² + n² = 1.

concepts.title: Equation of a line
concepts.text: A line through position vector a⃗ and parallel to b⃗ is r⃗ = a⃗ + λb⃗. Component equations lead directly to its Cartesian symmetric form.

concepts.title: Relative position of lines
concepts.text: Proportional directions give parallel or coincident lines. Non-proportional lines may intersect if their component equations have a common solution; otherwise they may be skew.

concepts.title: Shortest distance
concepts.text: The shortest joining segment is perpendicular to both line directions. A cross product supplies the common perpendicular direction and leads to compact distance formulas.

formulas: Line through a⃗ parallel to b⃗: r⃗ = a⃗ + λb⃗
Cartesian form: (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c
cos θ = |b⃗₁ · b⃗₂|/(|b⃗₁||b⃗₂|) for the acute angle between two lines
Parallel-line distance = |(a⃗₂ − a⃗₁) × b⃗|/|b⃗|
Non-parallel-line distance = |(a⃗₂ − a⃗₁) · (b⃗₁ × b⃗₂)|/|b⃗₁ × b⃗₂|
Lines are coplanar when (a⃗₂ − a⃗₁) · (b⃗₁ × b⃗₂) = 0
method: Extract one point and one direction vector from each line.
First test whether the direction vectors are proportional.
For a possible intersection, equate components and solve the parameters consistently.
For shortest distance, use the parallel or non-parallel formula only after classifying the lines.

example.question: Find the shortest distance between r⃗ = λ(î + ĵ) and r⃗ = k̂ + μ(î + ĵ).
steps: The common direction is b⃗ = î + ĵ, so the lines are parallel.
The difference between chosen points is d⃗ = k̂.
d⃗ × b⃗ = −î + ĵ, whose magnitude is √2; |b⃗| = √2.

practice.question: Write the direction cosines for direction ratios 1, 2, 2.
Write the line through (1, −2, 3) parallel to 2î + ĵ − k̂.
Find the angle between directions (1, 1, 0) and (1, −1, 0).
Check whether r⃗ = λ(î + ĵ) and r⃗ = î + ĵ + μ(î − ĵ) intersect.
practice.answer: They intersect at î + ĵ, the point (1, 1, 0).

practice.question: Find the distance between r⃗ = λî and r⃗ = ĵ + μî.
Find the foot from (1, 1, 1) to r⃗ = λ(î + ĵ + k̂).
practice.answer: The point already lies on the line, so the foot is (1, 1, 1) and the distance is 0.

tips: Direction ratios are not unique; direction cosines are normalised ratios with a chosen orientation.
Use the same parameter within one line but different parameters for different lines.
A zero shortest distance for non-parallel lines means they intersect.
Equations of planes and angles involving planes are outside the current syllabus.

notes.subtitle: Constraints, Feasible Regions & Optimisation

concepts.title: Decision variables and objective
concepts.text: Decision variables represent the unknown quantities. The objective function is a linear expression whose maximum or minimum models the stated goal.

concepts.title: Constraints and half-planes
concepts.text: Each linear inequality selects one side of its boundary line. Non-negativity conditions usually restrict the model to the first quadrant.

concepts.title: Feasible region
concepts.text: The feasible region is the intersection of all selected half-planes. It may be bounded, unbounded or empty; every feasible solution lies in or on it.

concepts.title: Corner-point principle
concepts.text: When a finite optimum exists, at least one corner point attains it. Equal optimum values at adjacent vertices make every point on their joining edge optimal.

formulas: Objective function: Z = ax + by
A boundary line is obtained by replacing ≤ or ≥ in a constraint by =
Feasible region = common intersection of all constraint half-planes
At each corner (x, y), objective value = ax + by
Equal optimum values at adjacent vertices imply multiple optimal solutions along that edge
method: Define the decision variables and state that they are non-negative.
Translate every resource or demand statement into a linear inequality.
Draw each boundary line from reliable intercepts and test a point to choose its half-plane.
List the feasible corner points, evaluate the objective at each, and interpret the best value in context.

example.question: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≤ 2, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
steps: The corresponding values of Z are 0, 6, 10 and 8.

practice.question: Test whether (2, 1) satisfies x + 2y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Write the constraint: each item uses 3 hours and at most 48 hours are available.
Find the intercepts of 2x + 3y = 12.
Maximise Z = x + y over vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, 3), (0, 2).
Explain what an empty feasible region means.
practice.answer: The constraints are inconsistent, so no feasible solution exists.

practice.question: Maximise Z = 2x + 4y subject to x + 2y ≤ 8, x + y ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0.
practice.answer: Maximum 16 at every point on the segment from (4, 2) to (0, 4).

tips: A boundary line is not the feasible region; shade only the common side of every constraint.
An unbounded feasible region does not automatically mean that no finite optimum exists.
Check all feasible vertices, including intersections with the axes.
The graphical syllabus uses two variables and at most three non-trivial constraints; simplex methods are outside scope.

notes.subtitle: Conditional Probability, Independence & Bayes’ Theorem

concepts.title: Conditional probability
concepts.text: P(A | B) measures the chance of A after learning that B occurred. The conditioning event becomes the reduced sample space and must have positive probability.

concepts.title: Multiplication and independence
concepts.text: The multiplication theorem builds an intersection through conditional probability. Independent events leave each other’s probabilities unchanged.

concepts.title: Total probability
concepts.text: A partition breaks the sample space into disjoint exhaustive cases. Add the probability of reaching the event through each case.

concepts.title: Bayes’ theorem
concepts.text: Bayes’ theorem reverses conditioning. It updates the prior probability of each cause after observing a result.

formulas: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), where P(B) > 0
P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B | A) = P(B)P(A | B)
A and B independent ⇔ P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
For a partition B₁, …, Bₙ: P(A) = ΣP(Bᵢ)P(A | Bᵢ)
P(Bⱼ | A) = P(Bⱼ)P(A | Bⱼ)/ΣP(Bᵢ)P(A | Bᵢ)
method: Name the events and identify clearly which event is conditioned on which.
Draw a probability tree when an experiment occurs in stages or through several sources.
Use total probability to find the overall observed-event probability before applying Bayes’ theorem.
Check that branch probabilities sum to 1 and that the final answer lies from 0 to 1.

example.question: A factory supplies 70% of items with a 2% defect rate; another supplies 30% with a 5% defect rate. Given a defect, find the probability it came from the second factory.

practice.question: If P(A ∩ B) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.5, find P(A | B).
Independent A and B have probabilities ½ and ⅕. Find P(A ∩ B).
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Find P(second red | first red) without replacement.
Sources X and Y supply ¾ and ¼ of items; defect rates are 2% and 6%. Find P(defect).
Using the previous data, find P(Y | defect).
Two cards are drawn without replacement. Find the probability both are aces.

tips: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are generally different.
Mutually exclusive positive-probability events are not independent.
Without replacement usually creates dependence; with replacement often restores independence.
Random variables and probability distributions are outside the current CBSE chapter scope.
